newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian bourse turnover seen exceeding target.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian bourse turnover seen exceeding target.

text.p: The volume of trade on the Nigerian stock market is on course to surpass the target for the year, dealers said on Friday.
Despite the recent fall in the prices of blue chips, they said turnover was set to reach seven billion naira worth of shares by the end of 1996.
This will quadruple the 1.8 billion naira for the whole of 1995, analysts said.
Already a turnover of more than 5.61 billion naira was achieved in October, according to stock market figures.
"The target is achievable," said a senior official of the Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE).

"With the recent upswing in the fortune of some leading shares, it may even exceed the target," he said, adding "The reversal of Nigerian Breweries fortunes is a positive trend. Guinness too has turned around."
Market operators said the projection was realistic in light of recent mergers.
They said it was also the time of the year when institutional investors were active in the share market.
"With the new issues recently listed and quite a few heavy transactions done lately, a seven billion naira turnover is attainable," said James Odife of Centre-point Investments Ltd.
"I will be more conservative and say 6.5 billion naira," said another dealer.
Traders said the volume of trade could have been even higher if the central securities clearing system were in operation early this year as originally planned.
The system's software was installed only this week by a team of Canadian experts after several delays.
When operational next year, operators said, it would cut costs and the period of transactions and help raise turnover.
According to the stock exchange some innovations introduced this year have already impacted positively on turnover.

It abolished the administrative allocation of shares for sale on the trading floor on March 1, followed by introduction of a maximum five percent daily price movement from the 20 kobo limit up or down in force before.
Settlement period was also halved to five days from 10 and the NSE says the target is three days settlement in 1997 to bring the exchange nearer to international standards.
The NSE came under criticism from the government this year, which blamed it for failing to internationalise the market in order to attract badly needed foreign investments.
The exchange, in turn, urged the government to further privatise Nigeria's inefficient and large public companies such as the electricity and telecommunications agencies.
Privatisation of the two is widely expected to take place next year with the potential of further boosting the volume of trade on the exchange. ($1=80 naira)
